title: Factuality vs. Fluency
excerpt: Learn why an AI response can sound excellent while still being factually wrong.
content:
An AI response can be fluent, confident, and easy to read while still containing incorrect information. This is one of the most important distinctions in AI evaluation.

Fluency is not factuality

Fluency measures how naturally the response communicates. Factuality asks whether the claims in the response are actually correct.

A useful evaluator should therefore avoid treating polished language as evidence that an answer is true.

What should you check?

  • Are the factual claims correct?
  • Does the response contradict the available reference?
  • Does it invent information that was not supported?
  • Does it confidently state something uncertain as fact?
A fluent answer can still be a failed answer. Evaluate what the model claims, not just how well it says it.

Practical evaluation

When evaluating factuality, separate the quality of the writing from the truth of the claims. Score them independently whenever your evaluation requires both dimensions.

title: How to Build an Evaluation Rubric
excerpt: Turn vague judgments about AI quality into clear criteria that can be evaluated consistently.
content:
A good evaluation rubric converts a subjective question such as “Is this answer good?” into specific criteria that different evaluators can apply consistently.

Start with the evaluation goal

First define what you actually want to measure. A customer-support assistant may need to be evaluated for factuality, relevance, completeness, tone, and policy compliance.

Define each dimension

Each dimension should describe one measurable quality. Avoid combining several unrelated properties into a single score.

Define failure conditions

A strong rubric should make it clear what counts as a failure and, where possible, what evidence should support the decision.

  • Criterion
  • Expected behavior
  • Failure condition
  • Evidence requirement
  • Score or verdict
The best rubric is not the longest one. It is the one that produces consistent decisions.

title: What Is Pairwise Evaluation?
excerpt: Learn how comparing two AI responses can reveal quality differences that absolute scoring may miss.
content:
Pairwise evaluation compares two candidate responses to the same task and asks which response performs better according to a defined criterion.

Why compare instead of score?

Absolute scores can be difficult to calibrate. Asking an evaluator to choose between two responses can sometimes make quality differences easier to identify.

What can you compare?

  • Factuality
  • Instruction following
  • Relevance
  • Completeness
  • Safety
  • Overall preference

The key is to keep the comparison criterion clear. “Which answer is better?” is less useful than “Which answer follows the user's instructions more completely?”

title: Evaluating RAG Grounding
excerpt: Understand how to determine whether an AI answer is actually supported by the retrieved context.
content:
Retrieval-augmented generation introduces another evaluation question: did the model actually base its answer on the information retrieved for it?

Three things can go wrong

  • The wrong context can be retrieved.
  • The correct context can be retrieved but the model can misunderstand it.
  • The answer can introduce claims that the context does not support.

Grounding evaluation

Grounding focuses on whether the claims made by the generated answer are supported by the available context.

Correct retrieval does not automatically produce a correct answer.

A useful RAG evaluation should therefore distinguish retrieval quality from answer quality and grounding.

title: Detecting Prompt Injection
excerpt: Learn the basic evaluation approach for testing whether an AI system follows untrusted instructions.
content:
Prompt injection occurs when untrusted content attempts to influence an AI system's behavior in ways that conflict with its intended instructions.

What should an evaluator test?

Evaluation should examine whether the system distinguishes trusted instructions from untrusted content and whether it maintains the intended policy when conflicting instructions appear.

Look for behavior, not just refusal

A safe system does not necessarily need to refuse every unusual request. The important question is whether it follows the correct instruction hierarchy and avoids unsafe behavior.

title: How to Evaluate AI Agents
excerpt: Move beyond response quality and learn how to evaluate planning, tool use, decisions, and task completion.
content:
AI agents are different from simple question-answering systems because they can plan, use tools, take actions, and operate across multiple steps.

Evaluate the complete task

An agent can produce a reasonable final message while still making serious errors during execution.

  • Did it understand the goal?
  • Did it choose the correct tool?
  • Did it use the tool correctly?
  • Did it maintain the required constraints?
  • Did it complete the task?

Agent evaluation therefore needs to examine both the final result and the path taken to reach it.
